pos: n. (a vessel in which things are pounded with a pestle; distinct from the morter of brick and stone)
etymology: Latin mortarium, a bowl for pounding. English keeps two words of the same origin: the vessel, and the morter of lime and sand that binds masonry, which the Authorized Version spells with an e.
biblical_def: The manna was prepared like grain: “And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil” (Num 11:8). Bread from heaven still had to be gathered, ground and baked; God gave the substance and left the labour, which is the pattern of nearly every providence He grants. The other use is one of the bleakest proverbs in Scripture: “Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him” (Pro 27:22). Grain is separated from its husk by pounding; a fool is not separated from his folly by any pressure whatever. The verse is a limit written into the book of wisdom itself — there are men whom instruction, humiliation, loss and pain will not change, because the folly is not a husk around them but the thing itself. What Proverbs says cannot be pounded out, the gospel says can only be replaced: a new heart also will I give you.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mortar as a vessel of wood or metal in the form of an inverted bell, in which substances are pounded or bruised with a pestle.
webster_full: MORTAR, n. [L. mortarium.] A vessel of wood or metal, in form of an inverted bell, in which substances are pounded or bruised with a pestle.
Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar. Prov. xxvii.
2. A short piece of ordnance, thick and wide, used for throwing bombs.
MORTAR, n. [See Morter.] A mixture of lime and sand with water, used as a cement for building.
scriptures: Num 11:8
And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil.
Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.
Exo 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.
Pro 6:9
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?
corruption_summary: It is assumed that any man can be improved by enough pressure — therapy, consequence, or education — and Proverbs 27:22 says flatly that some cannot.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole apparatus of modern correction rests on a premise Proverbs denies: that folly is a layer over a sound man, and that with sufficient pressure — a prison term, a programme, a season of hardship — the layer comes away and the sound man appears. Solomon has watched the process and reports the result. Bray him in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, and his foolishness will not depart from him. That is not cynicism and it is not despair; it is the wisdom literature refusing to promise what it cannot deliver, and it stands in the same book that commends instruction, correction and the rod. What Proverbs will not say is that means are causes. Circumstance can restrain a fool and cannot convert one.

The doctrine this exposes is regeneration, and it is why the Reformed churches have always insisted that the gospel is not an improvement scheme. Ezekiel does not promise a scoured heart but a new one: I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. Our Lord told a ruler of the Jews that a man must be born again, and answered his bewilderment by comparing the Spirit to the wind, which bloweth where it listeth. If folly could be pounded out, the cross would be a severe waste. And the practical comfort of the doctrine is considerable for anyone who has spent years applying pressure to a person he loves. The pestle was never going to do it. Prayer for a new heart is not the last resort after the methods fail; it is the only thing that was ever going to work, and it may be begun on the first day.
roots_summary: Hebrew medokah (H4085), a mortar for pounding, at Numbers 11:8; maktesh (H4388), a mortar, at Proverbs 27:22; distinct from chomer (H2563), the clay morter of brickmaking.
roots_lines: Hebrew medokah (H4085) — a mortar; they beat the manna in a mortar; Numbers 11:8.
Hebrew maktesh (H4388) — a mortar, a hollow; bray a fool in a mortar with a pestle; Proverbs 27:22.
Hebrew chomer (H2563) — clay, morter; the bondage of Egypt in morter and in brick; Exodus 1:14.
Hebrew ivveleth (H200) — folly, foolishness; what the pestle cannot separate from the man; Proverbs 27:22.
Hebrew leb chadash — a new heart; the only remedy Scripture offers for the fool; Ezekiel 36:26.
usage: “Beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans” — bread from heaven, and labour still required.
“Bray a fool in a mortar… yet will not his foolishness depart” — the limit of pressure.
“In morter, and in brick” — the other mortar, and the bondage it names.

pos: n. (calcined limestone, made by burning; in Scripture the figure of a people burned and the residue of a desecrated corpse)
etymology: Old English lim, cement or birdlime. Lime is produced by burning limestone or bones in a kiln, and both of Scripture's uses turn on the burning rather than on the building.
biblical_def: Isaiah uses lime for the fate of a people under judgment: “And the people shall be as the burnings of lime: as thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire” (Isa 33:12). Anyone who had seen a lime kiln knew the picture — stone reduced to white powder by a heat that does not go out quickly. The chapter draws the terrifying question from it: “Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?” (Isa 33:14), and answers it in the next verse with a description of the man who walks righteously and speaks uprightly. Amos uses the word for a war crime: “For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime” (Amo 2:1). Moab is not judged for something done to Israel but for the desecration of an enemy king's bones — and Edom was no friend of God's people either. God holds the nations to account for what they do to each other, and the sentence follows: “I will send a fire upon Moab” (Amo 2:2). He who burned bones is burned.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lime as a substance obtained from limestone or shells by expelling the carbonic acid by heat; quicklime; a principal ingredient in mortar and cement.
webster_full: LIME, n. A viscous substance; birdlime.
2. Calx; oxyd of calcium; the substance which is obtained from limestone, chalk or shells, by expelling from them the carbonic acid, by means of a strong heat.
The people shall be as the burnings of lime. Isa. xxxiii.
LIME, v.t. To smear with lime; to cement; to manure with lime.
scriptures: And the people shall be as the burnings of lime: as thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire.
The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?
Amo 2:1
Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime:
Amo 2:2
But I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the palaces of Kerioth: and Moab shall die with tumult, with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet:
corruption_summary: Everlasting burnings are treated as an image the church has outgrown, though Isaiah puts the phrase in the mouths of terrified worshippers inside Zion.
corruption_paragraphs: The most striking thing about Isaiah 33:14 is who is speaking. It is not the heathen but the sinners in Zion and the hypocrites — men inside the covenant community, in the place of worship, who are suddenly afraid. Their question is not rhetorical: who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings? The doctrine of eternal punishment is under steady pressure in our time from annihilationism, which says the wicked are extinguished, and from universalism, which says all are finally saved; and both are advanced on the ground that everlasting burnings are unworthy of a God of love. Isaiah's phrase is not an isolated Old Testament severity. Our Lord Jesus spoke more of the fire that is not quenched than any prophet, and He is the one who spoke of everlasting punishment in the same sentence as life eternal, using one adjective for both.

Isaiah does not leave the question unanswered, and the answer is the pastoral point. The next verse describes the man who dwells with the devouring fire: he that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes, that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil. That is not a scheme of salvation by works — the chapter's whole hope is the LORD who is our judge, our lawgiver and our king — but it is a plain statement that the redeemed are marked by a life. And Amos supplies the other half of the doctrine: God judges nations for what they do to nations, even outside the covenant, even to enemies of His own people. Moab burned Edom's king to lime, and the God of Israel took it up as His own quarrel.
roots_summary: Hebrew siyd (H7875), lime, from a root meaning to boil up or effervesce — the reaction of quicklime with water; used at Isaiah 33:12, Amos 2:1, and of the plaistered stones at Deuteronomy 27.
roots_lines: Hebrew siyd (H7875) — lime, plaister; the burnings of lime, and Moab's crime; Isaiah 33:12, Amos 2:1.
Hebrew mishrephoth — burnings; the kiln image behind the figure; Isaiah 33:12.
Hebrew moqed olam — everlasting burnings; the phrase spoken by the sinners in Zion; Isaiah 33:14.
Hebrew pesha (H6588) — transgression, rebellion; for three transgressions of Moab, and for four; Amos 2:1.
Greek aionios (G166) — everlasting, eternal; used of punishment and of life in one verse; Matthew 25:46.
usage: “The people shall be as the burnings of lime” — stone reduced to powder in a kiln.
“Who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?” — asked by men inside Zion.
“He burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime” — and God took it up as His own quarrel.

pos: n. pl. (toothed cutting tools; used in Scripture for dressing temple stone and, terribly, upon men)
etymology: Old English sagu, akin to Latin secare, to cut. The Hebrew megerah is a saw of iron; the same tool appears in Solomon's quarry and in David's treatment of Ammon.
biblical_def: Solomon's stones were cut with them: “All these were of costly stones, according to the measures of hewed stones, sawed with saws, within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping, and so on the outside toward the great court” (1Ki 7:9). The dressing was done in the quarry, so that “there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building” (1Ki 6:7) — every cut made elsewhere, and the temple rising in silence. The other use is one of the hardest verses in the histories: “And he brought out the people that were in it, and cut them with saws, and with harrows of iron, and with axes. Even so dealt David with all the cities of the children of Ammon” (1Ch 20:3). Scripture records the deeds of its heroes without softening them; David is the man after God's own heart and this is also in his account. Hebrews then puts the tool in the roll of the faithful: “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword” (Heb 11:37) — the same iron, used on the servants of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a saw as an instrument for cutting, consisting of a blade or thin plate of iron or steel, with one edge dentated or toothed.
webster_full: SAW, n. An instrument for cutting or dividing substances, as wood or stone, consisting of a blade, plate or ribbon of steel with one edge dentated or toothed.
Sawed with saws, within and without. 1 Kings vii.
SAW, v.t. To cut with a saw; to separate with a saw.
SAW-PIT, n. A pit over which timber is sawed by two men.
scriptures: All these were of costly stones, according to the measures of hewed stones, sawed with saws, within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping, and so on the outside toward the great court.

And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.

And he brought out the people that were in it, and cut them with saws, and with harrows of iron, and with axes. Even so dealt David with all the cities of the children of Ammon. And David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
corruption_summary: Scripture's refusal to sanitise David is used to discredit the Bible, when the honesty is one of the strongest evidences that it is not a book men wrote to flatter themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: A book composed to glorify a dynasty does not record that its founder committed adultery, arranged a murder, numbered the people against counsel, failed as a father, and dealt with the cities of Ammon as 1 Chronicles 20:3 describes. Scripture's pattern is to tell what happened and let the reader weigh it against the law it has already given. Two errors are made in response. The first is to treat every recorded act of a good man as approved — as though narration were commendation — which produces monstrous defences of things the Bible never defends. The second is to conclude that a book containing such acts cannot be from God. Both miss the point of the histories, which is that God works through men who are not righteous in themselves, and that the throne of David finds its true occupant only in David's greater Son.

The temple stones are the other lesson and they are worth keeping together with the first. All the cutting — hammer, axe, saw, every tool of iron — was done in the quarry, so that no sound of a tool was heard in the house while it was in building. The stones arrived shaped and were laid in silence. Peter says believers are lively stones, built up a spiritual house, and the figure is exact: the shaping happens where the noise is, in the ordinary trouble of a life, and the fitting is quiet. Hebrews 11 completes the picture in the darkest way. The same saws that dressed stones for the house of God were used on men who would not accept deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection — and the chapter says the world was not worthy of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew megerah (H4050), a saw; used of the stones of the temple and of the instruments turned on Ammon; Greek prizo (G4249), to saw asunder, at Hebrews 11:37.
roots_lines: Hebrew megerah (H4050) — a saw; sawed with saws, within and without; 1 Kings 7:9, 1 Chronicles 20:3.
Hebrew gazith (H1496) — hewn stone; the costly stones measured and dressed; 1 Kings 7:9.
Hebrew charits (H2757) — a sharp instrument, a harrow; with the saws in 1 Chronicles 20:3.
Greek prizo (G4249) — to saw in two; they were sawn asunder; Hebrews 11:37.
Greek lithos zon — a living stone; ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house; 1 Peter 2:5.
usage: “Sawed with saws, within and without” — the cutting done in the quarry.
“Neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house” — the house rose in silence.
“They were sawn asunder” — the same iron, on the servants of God.

pos: n. pl. (machines of war; siege artillery invented by cunning men, on the towers of Jerusalem and against the walls of Tyre)
etymology: Old French engin, from Latin ingenium, natural capacity or contrivance — the same root as ingenious. An engine is first a piece of cleverness and only afterwards a machine.
biblical_def: Uzziah armed Jerusalem with them: “And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men, to be on the towers and upon the bulwarks, to shoot arrows and great stones withal. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong” (2Ch 26:15). Every clause of that verse is approving until the last four words, and then the Chronicler turns: “But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense” (2Ch 26:16). He was struck with leprosy at the altar and dwelt in a several house until his death. Ezekiel uses the same word of the machines that would come against Tyre: “And he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers” (Eze 26:9). The instruments Uzziah invented for defence appear in the prophets as the instruments by which cities fall. Zechariah gives the rule that governs both: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an engine as any mechanical instrument or complicated machine; and particularly, a military machine for throwing stones or darts, or for battering walls.
webster_full: ENGINE, n. [Fr. engin; L. ingenium.] In a general sense, any instrument; more especially, any mechanical instrument or complicated machine.
2. A military machine; as a battering ram, or the like, used in ancient times.
He made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men. 2 Chron. xxvi.
3. Any instrument to effect a purpose; means; as, an engine of mischief.
scriptures: And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men, to be on the towers and upon the bulwarks, to shoot arrows and great stones withal. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong.
But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.
Eze 26:9
And he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Technical achievement is treated as a neutral good or as a wickedness in itself, while 2 Chronicles 26 credits the invention to God's help and then names what strength did to the man who held it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two hasty readings are available and both fail. The first treats Uzziah's engines as morally weightless — tools are tools, and only their use is good or bad. The Chronicler will not have it, because he attributes the success itself to God: he was marvellously helped, till he was strong. The skill of cunning men, the design of the machines, the spread of his name — all of it is help given. The second reading treats invention as the sin, as though ingenuity were a kind of Babel. The text does not say so. What it says is far more searching: the help was real, the strength was real, and the strength is what ruined him. But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. The danger was not in the engines but in what the possession of them did to a man's estimate of himself.

What Uzziah did with his strength is the detail that matters, and it is a matter of worship. He went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense — a thing lawful only for the sons of Aaron. Eighty priests withstood him, and he was wroth with them, and while he was wroth the leprosy rose in his forehead. A king who had built a nation's defences concluded that the ordinary boundaries of God's worship did not apply to a man of his stature. That is the standing temptation of every successful builder in the church, and the regulative principle exists precisely to prevent it: what God has appointed in worship is not adjustable by achievement. Zechariah's word to Zerubbabel is the corrective given to a man who was building with far less at his disposal — not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
roots_summary: Hebrew chishshabon (H2810), an invention or contrivance, of Uzziah's engines; mechi qobollo, an engine of war, at Ezekiel 26:9; with gabahh leb, the heart lifted up.
roots_lines: Hebrew chishshabon (H2810) — a device, an invention; engines invented by cunning men; 2 Chronicles 26:15.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, to devise; the root behind the cunning men and their contrivance.
Hebrew gabahh (H1361) — to be high, to be lifted up; his heart was lifted up to his destruction; 2 Chronicles 26:16.
Hebrew maal (H4603) — to trespass, to act unfaithfully; he transgressed against the LORD his God; 2 Chronicles 26:16.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit; not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit; Zechariah 4:6.
usage: “Engines, invented by cunning men” — skill counted as help given.
“He was marvellously helped, till he was strong” — the hinge of the whole reign.
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” — said to a man with nothing like Uzziah's resources.

pos: n. (a fortification, a stronghold; in the Authorized Version the defence itself rather than the ammunition)
etymology: Latin munitio, a fortifying, from munire, to wall or defend. The English word later shifted to mean ammunition; in the Authorized Version it keeps the older sense of the wall a city keeps.
biblical_def: Isaiah uses it of Jerusalem under siege: “And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision” (Isa 29:7). The armies that seemed unanswerable will prove as substantial as a dream a man wakes from. Nahum uses it in a burst of four commands to a doomed city: “He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily” (Nah 2:1). Every order is sound military advice, and Nineveh is going to fall anyway; the prophet is speaking with the terrible irony of a God who tells a city to do its best. The word therefore stands in Scripture at exactly the place where human defence is at its most competent and least sufficient. Isaiah 33 supplies what is the true munition: the place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks, said of the man who walks righteously, whose bread and water are sure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines munition as fortification, a place of defence, a stronghold; and secondarily, materials used in war, ammunition and military stores.
webster_full: MUNITION, n. [L. munitio, from munio, to fortify.] Fortification; a place of defence; a stronghold.
Keep the munition, watch the way. Nah. ii.
2. Ammunition; whatever materials are used in war for defence, or for annoying an enemy.
MUNIMENT, n. A fortification of any kind; a stronghold; a place of defence.
scriptures: Isa 29:7
And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision.
Nah 2:1
He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Psalm 127 is quoted to excuse doing nothing, though it names the builder, the watchman and their labour and denies only that the labour is what secures the result.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right relation between defence and dependence. Psalm 127 does not say that building and watching are useless; it says that except the LORD build and keep, they are in vain. The builder still builds. The watchman still wakes. Nahum tells Nineveh to keep the munition and watch the way, and every one of those imperatives is what a responsible city would do. What Scripture denies is that the wall is what saves. A Christian household, a congregation, a nation may take every prudent measure and must not then rest on the measures; and it may not use the doctrine of providence as a reason to leave the gate open.

Isaiah's image is the comfort. The nations that fight against Ariel and her munition shall be as a dream of a night vision — a hungry man dreaming that he eats, who wakes and is empty still. The armies were real enough to break a wall; before God they had no more substance than a dream. That is not a promise that every siege is lifted; Jerusalem did fall in Jeremiah's day, and the church has often been overrun. It is a statement about the final weight of things. The powers that press upon the people of God look solid and are not; and the defence that looks slight — the man who walks righteously, whose bread shall be given him and whose waters shall be sure — has his dwelling in the munitions of rocks. Nineveh kept her munition, watched her way, made her loins strong, and Nahum records the result three chapters long.
roots_summary: Hebrew metsurah (H4694) and matsor (H4692), a fortification, a siege-work; from tsur, to bind or besiege — the same root serving both the wall and the siege against it.
roots_lines: Hebrew metsurah (H4694) — a stronghold, a fortification; keep the munition; Nahum 2:1.
Hebrew matsod (H4685) — a siege work, a bulwark; all that fight against her and her munition; Isaiah 29:7.
Hebrew tsur (H6696) — to bind, to besiege; the root behind both the wall and the siege.
Hebrew misgab (H4869) — a high place, a defence; the LORD is a refuge and a high tower; Psalm 9:9.
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, to watch; except the LORD keep the city; Psalm 127:1.
usage: “All that fight against her and her munition… shall be as a dream of a night vision” — armies with the weight of a dream.
“Keep the munition, watch the way” — sound orders to a city that fell.
“Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” — and the watchman still wakes.

pos: n. pl. (the pivots on which a door turns; of gold in Solomon's temple, and the figure of the sluggard on his bed)
etymology: Middle English heng, from a root meaning to hang. The Hebrew poth denotes the socket or pivot on which an ancient door turned — not a modern hinge plate but the hollow the door-post spun in.
biblical_def: Two uses, and they could hardly be further apart. The temple: after the great vessels are listed — bowls, snuffers, basons, spoons, censers, all of pure gold — the inventory ends with “the hinges of gold, both for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, to wit, of the temple” (1Ki 7:50). The part nobody sees, the socket a door turns in, was gold. Nothing in the house of God was left cheap because it was hidden. Then Proverbs takes the same fitting for a picture of the sluggard: “As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed” (Pro 26:14). He is not motionless — he turns, with a good deal of activity — and he goes nowhere, because a door on its pivot has no other place to be. The next verse presses the joke further: “The slothful hideth his hand in his bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth” (Pro 26:15), and Proverbs asks the sluggard the only question worth asking him: “How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?” (Pro 6:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hinge as the hook or joint on which a door or gate turns; and figuratively, that on which anything depends or turns.
webster_full: HINGE, n. hinj. The hook or joint on which a door or gate turns.
2. That on which any thing depends or turns; a governing principle, rule or point.
As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed. Prov. xxvi.
HINGE, v.t. To furnish with hinges; to bend.
scriptures: And the bowls, and the snuffers, and the basons, and the spoons, and the censers of pure gold; and the hinges of gold, both for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, to wit, of the temple.
As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.
The slothful hideth his hand in his bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth.
Pro 6:9
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?
corruption_summary: Sloth has been reclassified as rest, and Proverbs' sluggard is the man who is never still and never arrives anywhere.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs is unusually witty about the sluggard and the wit is diagnostic. He turns on his bed like a door on its pivot — motion without travel. He hides his hand in his bosom and finds it too much trouble to bring it back to his mouth. He says there is a lion in the way. He is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason. Not one of these portraits is of a man doing nothing; they are of a man expending real energy on everything except the thing required. That is why the modern rehabilitation of sloth as rest does not fit. Scripture honours rest — it commands a sabbath, it says He giveth his beloved sleep, and the Lord told weary disciples to come apart into a desert place and rest a while. The sluggard is not resting. He is busy, and stationary.

The temple hinges are the answer to a related failure, which is doing well only what will be seen. Every visible vessel in Solomon's house was gold, and so were the pivots the doors turned in, hidden in the floor and the lintel, where no worshipper would ever look. The workmanship of God's house did not thin out where the eye stopped. That is the standard for a Christian's work: the accounts nobody audits, the preparation nobody sees, the promise kept when breaking it would never be discovered, the household run faithfully when there is no visitor. Colossians states it as a rule — whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men — and the hinges of gold are its picture. What holds a door up is what nobody photographs.
roots_summary: Hebrew poth (H6596), a socket or pivot for a door; with deleth (H1817), a door, and atsel (H6102), the slothful man of Proverbs.
roots_lines: Hebrew poth (H6596) — a hinge socket; the hinges of gold for the doors of the most holy place; 1 Kings 7:50.
Hebrew tsiyr (H6735) — a hinge, a pivot; as the door turneth upon his hinges; Proverbs 26:14.
Hebrew atsel (H6102) — slothful, sluggish; the standing figure of Proverbs; Proverbs 26:14, Proverbs 6:9.
Hebrew deleth (H1817) — a door; the doors of the inner house and of the temple; 1 Kings 7:50.
Hebrew zahab sagur — pure or shut-up gold; the metal of every vessel and of the hinges; 1 Kings 7:50.
usage: “The hinges of gold” — the part nobody sees, made of the same metal.
“As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed” — motion without travel.
“How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?” — the only question worth putting to him.

pos: n. pl. (channels; in Genesis the watering troughs where Jacob laid his peeled rods)
etymology: Old French gutiere, from Latin gutta, a drop — a channel for running water. The Hebrew rahat is the trough or runnel beside a well where flocks were watered.
biblical_def: Both occurrences belong to Jacob's long contest with Laban. “And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink” (Gen 30:38); and “whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods” (Gen 30:41). The watering trough was the one place a whole flock reliably gathered, and Jacob used it. Whether his method had any power at all the text never says; what it does say, in Jacob's own mouth a chapter later, is that God took away the cattle of Laban and gave them to him (Gen 31:9), and the angel of God had shown him in a dream what was happening. The gutters are therefore a small monument to a man's ingenuity in a situation he had every right to resent — his wages changed ten times — and to the fact that his ingenuity was not what prospered him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gutter as a channel at the eaves of a house for conveying water, and generally, any channel or hollow worn by running water.
webster_full: GUTTER, n. [Fr. gouttiere, from goutte, a drop; L. gutta.] A channel at the eaves of a roof for conveying away the rain.
2. A channel or passage for water; a hollow worn by a stream.
He set the rods… in the gutters in the watering troughs. Gen. xxx.
GUTTER, v.t. To cut or form into small hollows.
scriptures: And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink.
And it came to pass, whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods.
Gen 31:9
Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
corruption_summary: Jacob's rods in the gutters are treated as biblical endorsement of sympathetic magic, though the narrative reports the practice and assigns the result to God.
corruption_paragraphs: It is a standard charge that Genesis 30 teaches ancient folk-breeding — that looking at striped rods makes striped lambs. The chapter reports what Jacob did; it nowhere states that the rods caused the increase. The account is deliberately completed in the next chapter, where two witnesses give the true cause. The angel of God says in a dream, I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee; and Jacob tells his wives, God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me. Scripture frequently narrates without endorsing — Rachel's mandrakes, Gideon's ephod, Saul at Endor — and a reader who takes narration for approval will find the Bible teaching a great many things it plainly condemns elsewhere.

There is a quieter lesson in the location. The gutters were where the flocks came to drink, the one place the whole flock could be reached. Whatever we make of the rods, Jacob was working at the point of gathering, and men who wish to influence anything have always known to stand where people come for water. That is a fair description of preaching, of teaching children, of hospitality, of a well-kept table — and it is also a fair description of how the world shapes a household through what everyone in it drinks daily. Six years of this contest ended with Jacob rich and Laban resentful, and the honest summary is Jacob's own: except the LORD build the house, the builders labour in vain. He laboured, he schemed, he was cheated, and God gave the increase.
roots_summary: Hebrew rahat (H7298), a trough or gutter for watering flocks; with shoqeth (H8268), a watering trough, and maqqel (H4731), the rod Jacob peeled.
roots_lines: Hebrew rahat (H7298) — a trough, a channel; in the gutters in the watering troughs; Genesis 30:38.
Hebrew shoqeth (H8268) — a watering trough; from shaqah, to give drink; Genesis 30:38.
Hebrew maqqel (H4731) — a rod, a staff; the rods Jacob pilled and set up; Genesis 30:37.
Hebrew yacham (H3179) — to conceive, of flocks; that they should conceive when they came to drink; Genesis 30:38.
Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to strip away, to deliver; God hath taken away the cattle of your father; Genesis 31:9.
usage: “In the gutters in the watering troughs” — where the whole flock came.
“That they might conceive among the rods” — reported, and never credited.
“God hath taken away the cattle of your father” — the account Jacob himself gave.

pos: n. pl. (the wooden bowls in which dough was worked; carried out of Egypt bound up in the people's clothes)
etymology: English knead, Old English cnedan, to work dough, with trough. The Hebrew mishereth is a kneading bowl; the same word appears in the plague of frogs, which came up into the very bowls the bread was made in.
biblical_def: The word marks the hour of the exodus: “And the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders” (Exo 12:34). The detail is domestic and enormous. There was no time to let the dough rise, so they wrapped the bowls in their outer garments and put them on their shoulders, and the unleavened bread of the Passover was the result rather than the plan: “And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt, for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual” (Exo 12:39). The instruction had already anticipated the haste: “And thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover” (Exo 12:11). The same bowls had been a battlefield in the plagues, when the frogs came up into the houses, into the bedchambers and into the kneadingtroughs of Egypt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a kneading-trough as a trough or vessel in which dough is worked and mixed; and to knead as to work dough by pressing it with the hands.
webster_full: KNEAD, v.t. To work and press dough or paste into a mass, usually with the hands.
KNEADING, ppr. Working and mixing into a well mixed mass, as dough.
KNEADING-TROUGH, n. A trough or vessel in which dough is worked and mixed.
Their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes. Ex. xii.
scriptures: And the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders.

And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt, for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual.
And thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover.
Exo 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.
corruption_summary: The exodus is retold as a story of a people liberating themselves, when Exodus 12 has them thrust out with unrisen dough on their shoulders, having prepared no food at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation readings of the exodus — whether in liberation theology or in the general political use the story receives every generation — make Israel the agent of her own deliverance and the exodus a template for movements. The text resists this at every point, and the kneadingtroughs are the small proof. Israel did not organise a departure; they were thrust out, could not tarry, and had prepared for themselves no victual. Everything decisive was done by God: the plagues, the death of the firstborn, the blood on the lintel, the hardening and then the breaking of Pharaoh. The people obeyed an instruction about a lamb, and ate standing up with their shoes on. Their whole contribution to the night was to be ready to leave and to be under the blood.

The unleavened bread is the second point and it becomes doctrine. They ate unleavened because there was no time, and God then commanded the feast of unleavened bread for ever, so that the accident of the night became a memorial and afterwards a figure. Paul draws it out: purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us; therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Egypt's bondage had been in morter and brick, and the same hands that had made bricks under rigour now carried bowls of unrisen dough out into the desert. Deliverance in Scripture is rarely tidy, and it is never self-generated.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishereth (H4863), a kneading trough; with batseq (H1217), dough, and chippazon (H2649), haste — the word of the Passover's eating.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishereth (H4863) — a kneading trough; bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders; Exodus 12:34, Exodus 8:3.
Hebrew batseq (H1217) — dough; taken before it was leavened; Exodus 12:34.
Hebrew matstsah (H4682) — unleavened bread; the accident of a night made a perpetual feast; Exodus 12:39.
Hebrew chippazon (H2649) — haste, trepidation; ye shall eat it in haste; Exodus 12:11.
Greek zume (G2219) — leaven; purge out therefore the old leaven; 1 Corinthians 5:7.
usage: “Their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes” — the bowls went over the shoulder.
“They were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry” — not a departure they arranged.
“Ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD'S passover” — shoes on, staff in hand.

pos: n. (a shallow cooking vessel; one of the three appointed ways of preparing the meat offering)
etymology: English frying with pan. The Hebrew marchesheth is a deep pan or cauldron, distinguished in the law from the flat machabath and from the oven.
biblical_def: Leviticus lists three ways the meat offering might be prepared, and names the vessel each time: “And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in the fryingpan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil” (Lev 2:7); the others are the oven and the flat pan, and the same chapter opens with the uncooked form: “his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon” (Lev 2:1). Whichever way it came, the substance was the same — fine flour, oil, frankincense, no leaven and no honey, and salt in every offering. The priest took his handful, the memorial, and burned it upon the altar “of a sweet savour unto the LORD” (Lev 2:2), and the remainder was Aaron's and his sons'. The meat offering (which is a bread offering, not a flesh offering; meat in 1611 English means food) was the one bloodless offering, the gift of a man's labour and harvest. That God legislated for the poor man's frying pan as carefully as for the ram of consecration is the point worth carrying away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a frying-pan as a pan with a long handle, used for frying meats and other things over a fire.
webster_full: FRY, v.t. [L. frigo.] To dress food by roasting it in a pan over a fire.
FRYING, ppr. Dressing in a pan over a fire.
FRYING-PAN, n. A pan with a long handle, used for frying meat.
If thy oblation be a meat offering baken in the fryingpan. Lev. ii.
scriptures: Lev 2:7
And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in the fryingpan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.
Lev 2:1
And when any will offer a meat offering unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon:
Lev 2:2

And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons the priests: and he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar, to be an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD:
Pro 22:2
The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all.
corruption_summary: The ceremonial law is thought to concern only priests and spectacle, though Leviticus 2 legislates for a household pan and dignifies the offering a poor man could actually bring.
corruption_paragraphs: The meat offering is the offering of the ordinary man's produce, and the chapter goes out of its way to accommodate how he cooks. Oven, flat pan, frying pan, or simply fine flour poured with oil — each is named, each is acceptable, and the requirements are identical in every case: fine flour, oil, frankincense, salt, no leaven, no honey. God does not require a poor Israelite to acquire equipment he does not own in order to worship. That runs against a persistent instinct in religion, which is to make the acceptable offering the one that requires means. Leviticus is often caricatured as an elaborate machinery for the priestly caste; what it actually contains, again and again, is provision for what a man of small substance can bring, down to two turtledoves or two young pigeons where a lamb is out of reach.

What the offering signifies keeps it from being merely a peasant's convenience. Fine flour is grain crushed; oil runs through the whole of it; frankincense is added and burned; leaven, which sours and puffs, is excluded, and honey, which ferments, with it; salt, the sign of the covenant, is never lacking. It is a picture of a life presented to God — laboured for, refined, anointed, fragrant, without corruption — and it is answered in the one Man whose whole life was such an offering, and in the reasonable service Paul asks of believers, that we present our bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God. The priest burned a handful for a memorial and the rest fed Aaron's sons; the worshipper's gift became the ministers' bread, which is a quiet argument for the support of a faithful ministry from the offerings of the people.
roots_summary: Hebrew marchesheth (H4802), a deep pan or fryingpan; machabath (H4227), a flat plate; minchah (H4503), the meat offering itself — a gift or tribute.
roots_lines: Hebrew marchesheth (H4802) — a deep pan, a fryingpan; the third mode of preparing the meat offering; Leviticus 2:7, Leviticus 7:9.
Hebrew machabath (H4227) — a flat plate or griddle; the companion vessel; Leviticus 2:5.
Hebrew minchah (H4503) — a gift, a tribute, the meat offering; the bloodless offering of produce; Leviticus 2:1.
Hebrew soleth (H5560) — fine flour; the substance required whatever the vessel; Leviticus 2:7.
Hebrew azkarah (H234) — the memorial portion; the handful burned upon the altar; Leviticus 2:2.
usage: “A meat offering baken in the fryingpan” — the vessel a household already owned.
“Fine flour with oil” — the same substance whatever the cooking.
“The priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar” — a handful for God, the rest for His ministers.

pos: n. (a fine instrument for sewing; in the Gospels the eye through which a camel cannot pass)
etymology: Old English naedl. The Greek rhaphis in Matthew and Mark is a sewing needle; Luke, the physician, uses belone, a surgical needle. The saying is preserved in all three synoptic Gospels.
biblical_def: The Lord Jesus said it after the rich young ruler went away sorrowful: “And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God” (Mat 19:24). Mark gives it in the same words (Mar 10:25), and Luke with a physician's needle (Luk 18:25). The disciples' response shows how they understood it: they were exceedingly amazed, saying, Who then can be saved? — because in their world wealth was assumed to be a mark of God's favour and therefore an advantage in religion. The Lord's answer does not soften the saying but widens it: “With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” (Mat 19:26). That reply makes the camel a picture not merely of a rich man's difficulty but of every man's impossibility, and lays salvation entirely in the power of God. The largest beast in Palestine, and the smallest opening in a household — the Lord chose the two extremes on purpose.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a needle as a small instrument of steel, pointed at one end, with an eye at the other to receive a thread — used in sewing and embroidery.
webster_full: NEEDLE, n. A small instrument of steel, pointed at one end, with an eye at the other to receive a thread; used in sewing and embroidery.
2. A small pointed piece of steel, used in the mariner's compass.
3. Any thing in the form of a needle; as the needles of a pine tree.
It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. Matt. xix.
scriptures: And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.
It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.
For it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.
But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.
corruption_summary: The saying is defused by a legend about a low gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye, for which there is no evidence and which reverses the Lord's meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: A story circulates in pulpits that Jerusalem had a small night gate called the Needle's Eye, through which a camel could pass if it were unloaded and made to kneel — difficult, but possible with effort. There is no ancient evidence for such a gate; the tale appears to date from the Middle Ages and it survives because it is comfortable. It also destroys the passage. The disciples' question — Who then can be saved? — makes no sense if the Lord had merely said that rich men must try harder, and His answer, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible, is unanswerable proof that impossibility was the point. Any interpretation that leaves a man something to do to squeeze himself through has replaced the doctrine of salvation by grace with a doctrine of salvation by effort, and has done it in the very passage where the Lord excluded it.

The corollary corruption is the prosperity teaching, which does openly what the gate legend does quietly: it makes wealth a sign of God's approval and therefore an aid to faith. That was the disciples' assumption and the Lord overturned it. Riches are not called evil here — Abraham was rich, and Job, and Joseph of Arimathaea — but they are named as a hindrance so severe that only omnipotence overcomes it, because a man with much finds it nearly impossible to be poor in spirit. The pastoral use is not for sorting other people into camels and needles. It is for a Christian to ask what he actually trusts, since the ruler in the story kept commandments from his youth and went away sorrowful over one thing. And the promise stands over it all: with God all things are possible, which is the only hope any rich man — or any man — has ever had.
roots_summary: Greek rhaphis (G4476), a sewing needle, in Matthew and Mark; belone (G956), a surgical needle, in Luke; kamelos (G2574), a camel; trumalia (G5168), a hole or eye.
roots_lines: Greek rhaphis (G4476) — a needle for sewing; Matthew 19:24, Mark 10:25.
Greek belone (G956) — a needle, especially a surgeon's; used by Luke the physician; Luke 18:25.
Greek kamelos (G2574) — a camel; the largest common beast set against the smallest opening; Matthew 19:24.
Greek trumalia (G5168) — a hole, a perforation; the eye of the needle; Mark 10:25.
Greek adunatos (G102) — impossible, without power; with men this is impossible; Matthew 19:26.
usage: “Easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle” — the two extremes, chosen on purpose.
“Who then can be saved?” — the question the saying was meant to raise.
“With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” — the answer, and the doctrine.
